semantic_correction.stem: A healthy adult is considering living kidney donation. Which explanation by the nurse best describes the purpose of the donor evaluation?

options.A: It assesses the donor’s medical and psychosocial suitability, explains donation risks, and supports a voluntary informed decision with an independent donor advocate.
options.B: It mainly confirms compatibility with the recipient; once compatibility is established, donor psychosocial concerns have little effect on whether donation proceeds.
options.C: It is primarily a physical-health screening; psychological readiness and freedom from family pressure are addressed only when the donor reports concerns.
options.D: It determines whether donation will benefit the recipient enough to justify proceeding, even when the potential donor remains uncertain about donating.

semantic_correction.rationale: A is correct. Current HRSA-supported SRTR guidance states that potential living kidney donors complete a thorough medical and psychological evaluation to determine whether donation is appropriate and whether the donor is healthy enough to donate. The evaluation may include physical examination, compatibility testing, psychological assessment, and meeting with an Independent Living Donor Advocate (ILDA), who helps the donor understand risks and obtain resources needed to decide whether to donate. SRTR also states that the evaluation may address whether the decision is entirely the donor’s own and not the result of pressure, and that the donor may change their mind at any time. B is incorrect because donor medical and psychosocial suitability remain central after compatibility is assessed. C is incorrect because psychological readiness and voluntariness are core evaluation elements, not optional only when concerns are volunteered. D is incorrect because living donation remains voluntary and recipient benefit does not override the donor’s decision.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Explain that living kidney donor evaluation protects the potential donor through medical and psychosocial assessment, risk education, independent advocacy, and confirmation of voluntary informed decision-making.
semantic_correction.source_organization: Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) / Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients (SRTR)
semantic_correction.source_version_date: Current HRSA/SRTR living-donor resource accessed August 21, 2026
semantic_correction.source_locator: The Living Donor Journey → What to Expect: extensive multistep transplant-center evaluation and donor choice whether to continue. Kidney Transplants → Living Donor Evaluation: thorough medical and psychological evaluation; examples include physical examination, blood compatibility testing, psychological assessment, and meeting with an Independent Living Donor Advocate; the ILDA helps the donor understand living-donor risks and obtain resources needed to decide whether to donate; evaluation may assess whether the decision is entirely the donor’s own and not the result of pressure. FAQ → What is included in a donor evaluation?: physical health, compatibility, psychological preparedness, and the donor may change their mind at any time. FAQ → How do I get help navigating the donor evaluation process?: every transplant center is required to have an Independent Donor Advocate who promotes the donor’s best interests.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: Living kidney donor evaluation is a donor-protection process that includes medical and psychological assessment, risk discussion, independent donor advocacy, and confirmation that donation is voluntary rather than driven by recipient need or external pressure.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item directly tests the donor-protection purpose of living kidney donor evaluation with one clearly best answer, independent advocacy, voluntariness, and no length cue.

option_audit.A: Correct. Each element is directly supported by current HRSA/SRTR guidance: medical and psychosocial evaluation, risk education, voluntariness, and independent donor advocacy.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. Compatibility is only one part of evaluation; donor medical and psychosocial suitability remain essential to determining whether donation is appropriate.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Psychological readiness, informed decision-making, and freedom from pressure are integral evaluation concerns and are not contingent on the donor first volunteering a concern.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Recipient benefit does not override donor autonomy; the donor may change their mind during the process and the independent donor advocate promotes the donor’s best interests.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone captures the comprehensive donor-protection function of evaluation; B narrows evaluation to compatibility, C omits psychosocial/voluntariness assessment, and D subordinates donor autonomy to recipient benefit.
cueing_check: The choices are closely balanced in length (A 162, B 158, C 157, D 151 characters), use parallel explanatory statements, and no option is uniquely detailed or conspicuously longer than the others.
